items.front: Nesting of number sets, and examples of irrationals?
items.back: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R. Irrationals (non-terminating, non-repeating): √2, √3, π, e. √16 = 4 is rational.

items.front: Prime, composite, co-prime — the key facts?
items.back: 2 is the only even prime & smallest prime; 1 is neither prime nor composite; co-prime means HCF = 1 (e.g. 8 & 15).

items.front: Divisibility tests for 3/9, 4, 8, 11?
items.back: 3 & 9: digit sum divisible by 3/9. 4: last two digits. 8: last three digits. 11: (odd-place − even-place) sum = 0 or a multiple of 11.

items.front: How to count the factors of a number?
items.back: If N = p^{a}·q^{b}·r^{c}, number of factors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1), counting 1 and N. E.g. 360 = 2³·3²·5 → 4·3·2 = 24.
items.examPoint: Number of factors via prime factorisation

items.front: How to count odd (and even) factors?
items.back: Odd factors: drop all powers of 2, then take the (e+1) product. Even factors = total − odd. E.g. 1260 → odd = 3·2·2 = 12.

items.front: Unit-digit cyclicity of powers?
items.back: Only base's unit digit matters. 2,3,7,8 cycle with period 4; 4,9 with period 2; 0,1,5,6 stay fixed. Use (power mod 4).

items.front: Unit digit of a sum/product of powers — method?
items.back: Reduce each power to its unit digit via cyclicity, then add/multiply. E.g. 17^{23} + 24^{24} → 3 + 6 = 9.
items.examPoint: Unit digit of an expression (sum/product of powers)

items.front: Trailing zeros in n! — formula?
items.back: ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + … (5s are the limiting factor). E.g. 100! → 20 + 4 = 24 zeros.

items.front: Trailing zeros in a product/power — method?
items.back: Prime-factorise, total the 2s and 5s, take the minimum. E.g. 15^{50}·20^{40}·25^{30} → min(80, 150) = 80.

items.front: Remainder of a power (e.g. 2^{100} ÷ 7)?
items.back: List the power-remainders to find the cycle: 2, 4, 1 (length 3). 100 ÷ 3 leaves 1, so 2^{100} matches 2^{1} = 2. Remainder = 2.

items.front: Remainder shortcut when the divisor divides a larger divisor?
items.back: N ÷ d₁ leaves r; if d₂ | d₁ then N ÷ d₂ leaves r mod d₂. E.g. N÷899 leaves 63; 899 = 29·31 → N÷29 leaves 63 mod 29 = 5.
items.examPoint: Remainder — divisor as a multiple / successive division

items.front: HCF × LCM identity for two numbers?
items.back: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers (two numbers only). E.g. HCF 12, LCM 240, one number 48 → other = 2880/48 = 60.
items.examPoint: HCF × LCM = product of two numbers

items.front: How to compare/order fractions quickly?
items.back: Convert to decimals, or cross-multiply (a/b vs c/d → a·d vs b·c), or use a common denominator, then compare.

items.front: Convert a recurring decimal to a fraction?
items.back: Pure recurring 0.(block) = block / (as many 9s as digits). E.g. 0.363636… = 36/99 = 4/11. 0.7̄ = 7/9.

items.front: Perfect-square unit-digit test + HCF/LCM word problems?
items.back: Squares end only in 0,1,4,5,6,9 (never 2,3,7,8). Bells toll together → LCM; greatest number leaving same remainder → HCF of differences.

items.front: How do you test divisibility by 7?
items.back: Remove the last digit; subtract twice it from the rest; repeat. 0 or a multiple of 7 means divisible (343: 34 − 6 = 28).

items.front: How do you test divisibility by 13?
items.back: Remove the last digit; ADD four times it to the rest; repeat (351: 35 + 4 = 39 = 3 × 13).

items.front: Why is 256256 divisible by 7, 11 and 13?
items.back: abcabc = abc × 1001 and 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13. A four-digit repeat abab = ab × 101 is not.

items.front: How do you test a long number for 7, 11 or 13 at once?
items.back: Alternately add and subtract three-digit groups from the right (764 − 233 + 1 = 532); test that result.

items.front: Sum of all factors — formula and example?
items.examPoint: Number of factors via prime factorisation

items.front: Odd-factor trap: what must you drop first?
items.back: Every power of 2. 1260 = 2^{2} × 3^{2} × 5 × 7 has 12 odd factors; even = 36 − 12 = 24.

items.front: Trailing-zero trap for 125! or 625!?
items.back: Keep dividing by 125, 625 … : 125! = 25 + 5 + 1 = 31 zeros, not 30.

items.front: Remainder trap: N ÷ 6 leaves 5 — what does N ÷ 12 leave?
items.back: Cannot be fixed (5 or 11). The rule only works from a divisor down to its factor.
items.examPoint: Remainder — divisor as a multiple / successive division

items.front: Fermat's shortcut for a remainder of a power?
items.back: p prime, p not dividing a: a^{p−1} leaves 1. Reduce the exponent mod (p − 1): 5^{100} ÷ 7 → 5^{4} → 2.

items.front: Remainder of (d − 1)^{n} ÷ d?
items.back: 1 when n is even; d − 1 when n is odd (29^{51} ÷ 30 leaves 29).

items.front: Largest square tile for a floor — method?
items.back: HCF of length and breadth in the same unit; tiles = (L ÷ side)(B ÷ side). 1650 × 1200 cm → 150 cm, 88 tiles.
items.examPoint: HCF & LCM — word problems (bells, greatest divisor, least number)

items.front: Runners on a circular track meet at the start when?
items.back: After the LCM of their lap times (40, 60, 75 s → 600 s = 10 min), not the product.
items.examPoint: HCF & LCM — word problems (bells, greatest divisor, least number)

items.front: When does a fraction give a terminating decimal?
items.back: In lowest terms, its denominator has only 2s and 5s. Cancel first: 7/56 = 1/8 terminates.

items.front: How many terms in an evenly spaced list?
items.back: n = (last − first)/step + 1. 7, 13, …, 205 → 198/6 + 1 = 34. Do not drop the +1.
items.examPoint: Counting multiples / terms in a range (AP count)

items.front: Divisible by both 12 and 18 — count multiples of what?
items.examPoint: Counting multiples / terms in a range (AP count)

items.front: How many primes up to 100, and how do you test one number?
items.back: 25 primes up to 100. Test by primes up to √n: 391 needs up to 19 → 17 × 23.

items.front: Scientific-notation trap after multiplying or dividing?
Order-of-magnitude cut-off?
items.examPoint: Order of magnitude — nearest power of ten

items.front: Is 22/7 rational? Is 0.1010010001… rational?
items.back: 22/7 is rational (only approximates π). 0.1010010001… never repeats a fixed block, so irrational.
